Oct. 1, 2026
What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In that case, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
Advertisement
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Those in support include Secretary of State Shirley Weber, California Common Cause, the League of Women Voters of California and Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Opponents include nonprofit Election Integrity Project California, Inc.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The state Legislature was tasked with developing a better recall system after Gov. Gavin Newsom faced a gubernatorial challenge in 2021, costing state and local governments more than $200 million (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-02-03/california-recall-election-cost-200-million-dollars).
Newsom defeated the recall attempt after nearly 62% voted (https://www.latimes.com/projects/newsom-california-recall-election-live-results/) to keep him in office. Had he been ousted, conservative talk radio host Larry Elder was the leading candidate to replace him with less than 49% of the vote.
Former state Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled in 2018 and later reelected to office, co-authored the measure that made it to the ballot. He believes that the elimination of a second simultaneous vote for a replacement removes “the political incentive for gamesmanship around recalls.”
“My solution is really simple: It’s to eliminate that second question and maintain the recall as a valid, powerful tool of accountability,” he said.
Advertisement
It’s not uncommon for someone to get appointed to fill an official’s term if they leave office before their time is up. Newman said that slotting the lieutenant governor into the role of governor in the event of a recall would follow a precedent.
The lieutenant governor currently serves as acting governor when the governor leaves the state.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 5 would change the way recall elections are conducted in the state by prioritizing voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement. The ballot measure also would make a major change to gubernatorial recall elections by automatically designating the lieutenant governor as the replacement.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.
Oct. 1, 2026
What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In that case, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
Advertisement
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Those in support include Secretary of State Shirley Weber, California Common Cause, the League of Women Voters of California and Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Opponents include nonprofit Election Integrity Project California, Inc.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The state Legislature was tasked with developing a better recall system after Gov. Gavin Newsom faced a gubernatorial challenge in 2021, costing state and local governments more than $200 million (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-02-03/california-recall-election-cost-200-million-dollars).
Newsom defeated the recall attempt after nearly 62% voted (https://www.latimes.com/projects/newsom-california-recall-election-live-results/) to keep him in office. Had he been ousted, conservative talk radio host Larry Elder was the leading candidate to replace him with less than 49% of the vote.
Former state Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled in 2018 and later reelected to office, co-authored the measure that made it to the ballot. He believes that the elimination of a second simultaneous vote for a replacement removes “the political incentive for gamesmanship around recalls.”
“My solution is really simple: It’s to eliminate that second question and maintain the recall as a valid, powerful tool of accountability,” he said.
Advertisement
It’s not uncommon for someone to get appointed to fill an official’s term if they leave office before their time is up. Newman said that slotting the lieutenant governor into the role of governor in the event of a recall would follow a precedent.
The lieutenant governor currently serves as acting governor when the governor leaves the state.

I'm getting a good picture. Let me look deeper at:

1. The LA Times article on Prop 5 (Oct 1, 2026)
2. The SF Chronicle editorial (they seem critical — "flaw so bizarre even its author doesn't like it" — the flaw being that a recalled official can run in the special election to replace themselves)
3. The CalMatters coverage
4. The LA Times Skelton column (Yes)
5. McClatchy endorsement (Yes)
6. SCNG/Bay Area News Group (No)

Let me also look at the text of the proposed law, and think about the key facts:
- 2003 recall: Gray Davis recalled, Arnold Schwarzenegger won with ~48.6% of the replacement vote
- 2021 recall: Newsom survived; Larry Elder was leading replacement candidate
- Newman recalled in 2018 over gas tax vote

Key arguments for Yes:
- Closes loophole where replacement can win with small plurality (e.g., 2003: Schwarzenegger 48.6%; 2021: Elder would've won with ~28% of total recall voters... actually Elder got about 49% of the replacement vote, but among all voters in the election it was less)
- Most states use succession/special election
- Removes incentive for partisan gamesmanship
- Reduces costs by not having second question (though special elections could add costs)
- Endorsed by LWV, Common Cause, Dan Schnur (former FPPC chair)
- Sacramento Bee/Fresno Bee etc. (McClatchy) endorse
- LA Times Skelton: Yes

Key arguments for No:
- Takes power from voters to choose replacement
- Governor (often same party as recalled official... or not) appoints replacements for constitutional officers
- Special elections cost money and leave offices vacant
- Recalled official can run again in the special election to fill their own seat (the "bizarre flaw")
- Author Josh Newman was recalled himself — motive questions ("Newman's Revenge")
- SCNG editorial boards: No; SF Chronicle: appears to be No (or at least critical); Bay Area News Group: No
- Republican lawmakers opposed

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 5 would change the way recall elections are conducted in the state by prioritizing voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement. The ballot measure also would make a major change to gubernatorial recall elections by automatically designating the lieutenant governor as the replacement.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.
Oct. 1, 2026
What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In that case, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
Advertisement
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Those in support include Secretary of State Shirley Weber, California Common Cause, the League of Women Voters of California and Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Opponents include nonprofit Election Integrity Project California, Inc.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The state Legislature was tasked with developing a better recall system after Gov. Gavin Newsom faced a gubernatorial challenge in 2021, costing state and local governments more than $200 million (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-02-03/california-recall-election-cost-200-million-dollars).
Newsom defeated the recall attempt after nearly 62% voted (https://www.latimes.com/projects/newsom-california-recall-election-live-results/) to keep him in office. Had he been ousted, conservative talk radio host Larry Elder was the leading candidate to replace him with less than 49% of the vote.
Former state Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled in 2018 and later reelected to office, co-authored the measure that made it to the ballot. He believes that the elimination of a second simultaneous vote for a replacement removes “the political incentive for gamesmanship around recalls.”
“My solution is really simple: It’s to eliminate that second question and maintain the recall as a valid, powerful tool of accountability,” he said.
Advertisement
It’s not uncommon for someone to get appointed to fill an official’s term if they leave office before their time is up. Newman said that slotting the lieutenant governor into the role of governor in the event of a recall would follow a precedent.
The lieutenant governor currently serves as acting governor when the governor leaves the state.

Now I have a much fuller picture. Let me also check:
1. The CalMatters article (almanacnews one is a CalMatters syndication)
2. George Skelton's column (already summarized: Yes)
3. The Sacramento Bee (McClatchy) endorsement (Yes)
4. Maybe the CalMatters voter guide summary
5. The actual text of the law — the PDF from the SOS.

Key facts so far:
- The measure (SCA 1, Newman): removes second question from recall ballots
- Recall vacancies filled via existing vacancy rules
- Governor recalled → Lt. Gov. becomes Governor (until next statewide election if early in term, otherwise rest of term)
- Other statewide officials → Governor appoints
- Legislators → special election
- Recalled official CAN run in the special election to fill their own former seat (this reverses a constitutional ban)
- Fiscal impact: unknown, net could be savings or costs in the millions

Supporters: Secretary of State Shirley Weber, Common Cause, League of Women Voters, Dan Schnur (former FPPC chair), Lt. Gov. Kounalakis, McClatchy editorial boards (Sacramento Bee, Fresno Bee, etc.), George Skelton (LA Times columnist)
Opponents: Republican lawmakers (Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones, Assemblymember Joe Patterson), SCNG editorial boards (LA Daily News, Press-Telegram, OC Register?), Bay Area News Group (Mercury News, East Bay Times), Santa Cruz Sentinel (no), SF Chronicle (no — because of the "recalled official can run to replace themselves" provision), Election Integrity Project California

Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections. Voters get their say with Prop. 5
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)
October 5, 2026 5:00 am

Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat.
She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.”
A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms.
If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins.
“I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said.
California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election.
The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections.
However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions.
The “weak gazelle”
Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman.
In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 27 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes.
Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax.
“We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.”
Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes.
In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax.
Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate.
In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy.
“If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said.
But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911.
In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.”
Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill.
“I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.”
Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5.
Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change.
How would it work?
If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election.
If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election.
If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change.
“The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said.
He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections.
However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort.
“It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.”
A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.”
Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions.

This amendment proposed by Senate Constitutional

PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO
ARTICLES II AND V
First—That Section 15 of Article II thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 15. (a) An election to determine whether to
recall an officer and, if appropriate, to elect a successor
shall be called by the Governor and held not less than
60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of
certification of sufficient signatures.
(b) A recall election may be conducted within 180 days
from the date of certification of sufficient signatures in
order that the election may be consolidated with the
next regularly scheduled election occurring wholly or
partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall
election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote
at that next regularly scheduled election equal at least
50 percent of all the voters eligible to vote at the recall
election.
(c) If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the
officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the
candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The
officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any
candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d)
of Section 16 of Article VI. and the office shall be
vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with
this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer
who was the subject of the recall election shall not be
appointed to fill the vacancy in that office.

Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections. Voters get their say with Prop. 5
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)
October 5, 2026 5:00 am

This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat.
She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.”
A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms.
If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins.
“I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said.
California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election.
The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections.
However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions.
The “weak gazelle”
Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman.
In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 27 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes.
Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax.
“We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.”
Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes.
In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax.
Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate.
In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy.
“If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said.
But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911.
In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.”
Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill.
“I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.”
Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5.
Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change.
How would it work?
If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election.
If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election.
If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change.
“The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said.
He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections.
However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort.
“It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.”
A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.”
Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions.

In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.”
Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill.
“I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.”
Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5.
Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change.
How would it work?
If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election.
If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election.
If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change.
“The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said.
He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections.
However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort.
“It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.”
A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.”
Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions.

PROPOSITION 5
This amendment proposed by Senate Constitutional
Amendment 1 of the 2023–2024 Regular Session
(Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024) expressly
amends the California Constitution by amending
sections thereof; therefore, existing provisions
proposed to be deleted are printed in strikeout type
and new provisions proposed to be added are printed in
italic type to indicate that they are new.
PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO
ARTICLES II AND V
First—That Section 15 of Article II thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 15. (a) An election to determine whether to
recall an officer and, if appropriate, to elect a successor
shall be called by the Governor and held not less than
60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of
certification of sufficient signatures.
(b) A recall election may be conducted within 180 days
from the date of certification of sufficient signatures in
order that the election may be consolidated with the
next regularly scheduled election occurring wholly or
partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall
election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote
at that next regularly scheduled election equal at least
50 percent of all the voters eligible to vote at the recall
election.
(c) If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the
officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the
candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The
officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any
candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d)
of Section 16 of Article VI. and the office shall be
vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with
this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer
who was the subject of the recall election shall not be
appointed to fill the vacancy in that office.

Second—That Section 17 of Article II thereof is
amended to read:
SEC. 17. If recall of the Governor or Secretary of
State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be
performed by the Lieutenant Governor Secretary of
State or Controller, respectively. If recalls of the
Governor and Secretary of State are initiated at the
same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be
performed by the Controller.
Third—That Section 10 of Article V thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 10. (a) The Lieutenant Governor shall become
Governor when a vacancy occurs in the office of
Governor.
(b) Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 15 of
Article II, if the Governor is removed from office by
recall, the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor
for the remainder of the unexpired term. If the Governor
is removed from office by recall before the close of the
nomination period for the next statewide election during
the first two years of the Governor’s term, a special
election shall be called to replace the Governor and
shall be consolidated with the statewide primary
election and, if necessary, the subsequent statewide
general election. If a candidate receives a majority of
the votes in the special election that is consolidated
with the statewide primary election, that candidate
shall become Governor for the remainder of the
unexpired term. If no candidate receives a majority of
the votes, the top two vote-getters shall compete in a
special election consolidated with the subsequent
statewide general election, and the winner of that
election shall become Governor for the remainder of the
unexpired term.
(c) The Lieutenant Governor shall act as Governor
during the impeachment, absence from the State, or
other temporary disability of the Governor or of a
Governor-elect who fails to take office.
(d) The Legislature shall provide an order of
precedence after the Lieutenant Governor for
succession to the office of Governor and for the
temporary exercise of the Governor’s functions.
(e) The Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction to
determine all questions arising under this section.
(f) Standing to raise questions of vacancy or temporary
disability is vested exclusively in a body provided by
statute.

- Recall vacancies filled via existing vacancy rules
- Governor recalled → Lt. Gov. becomes Governor (until next statewide election if early in term, otherwise rest of term)

Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections. Voters get their say with Prop. 5

CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)

This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat.
She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.”
A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms.
If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins.
“I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said.
California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election.
The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections.
However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions.
The “weak gazelle”
Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman.
In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 27 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes.
Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax.
“We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.”
Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes.
In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax.
Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate.
In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy.
“If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said.
But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911.
In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.”
Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill.
“I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.”
Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5.
Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change.
How would it work?
If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election.
If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election.
If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change.
“The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said.
He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections.
However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort.
“It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.”
A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.”
Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions.

Now I have the actual text. Key details from the text:

1. Article II, Section 15(c): If the majority votes to recall, the officer is removed and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with the Constitution and statute, PROVIDED THAT the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office. (But note: the old text said "The officer may not be a candidate" — this is being struck out. So the recalled officer CAN be a candidate in the special election — matching what the Chronicle said. The new provision says they can't be appointed, but they can run in the special election.)

Wait, let me re-read. The text shows strikethrough in the original document, but this plain text version doesn't show strikethrough. Let me parse it:

Old text (Article II, Sec 15(c)): "If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 16 of Article VI."

New text: "If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the officer is removed and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."

So the old ban on the recalled officer being a candidate is removed. Under the new system:
- The recalled officer CAN run in the special election to fill their own former seat.
- The recalled officer CANNOT be appointed to fill the vacancy.

Interesting — so if a legislator is recalled, a special election is held, and the recalled legislator could run again in that special election. Same for governor: if the Governor is recalled in the first two years of the term, the Lt. Gov. becomes Governor and a special election is held (consolidated with the next statewide primary, then runoff at general). The recalled Governor could run in that special election.

Actually wait — for the Governor: if recalled early in term, the Lt. Gov. becomes Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term, BUT a special election is called to replace the Governor, consolidated with the statewide primary election. If a candidate receives a majority at the primary, they become Governor for the remainder. Otherwise top two compete at the general election.

Hmm, and can the recalled Governor run in that special election? The text says the officer who was the subject of the recall shall not be APPOINTED to fill the vacancy — but the ban on being a CANDIDATE is removed. So yes, the recalled Governor could run in the special election to fill their own office. This is the "bizarre flaw" the SF Chronicle mentioned.

2. Article V, Section 10(b): If the Governor is removed by recall, the Lt. Gov. becomes Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term. If the Governor is removed by recall before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, a special election shall be called to replace the Governor, consolidated with the statewide primary (and if necessary, subsequent statewide general election). Majority requirement at the primary; if no majority, top two compete at the general.

So the special election for governor is consolidated with existing scheduled elections — meaning it's NOT a standalone expensive election. That addresses some of the cost concern for gubernatorial recalls. For legislative recalls, the Governor calls a special election within about four months; those might need to be standalone in some cases (though often can be consolidated with scheduled elections).

Now the "no funds raised" point: "with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters' gut reactions." Also the SOS page: "No committees identified" for support or opposition. And PPIC poll: 59% likely no, 35% likely yes.

Also from CalMatters: How it works — governor calls special election within about four months to replace a recalled legislator. If a governor is recalled within first two years, the Secretary of State would call a special election. If in the second two years, Lt. Gov. finishes the term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. For statewide officials (treasurer, AG, insurance commissioner), the Governor appoints replacement to serve until next scheduled election.

Now let me consider who supports/opposes:
- Supporters: SOS Shirley Weber, Lt. Gov. Kounalakis, Common Cause, LWV, Dan Schnur (former FPPC chair, a Republican actually — he was Pete Wilson's aide), McClatchy editorial boards (Sac Bee, Fresno Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, SLO Tribune), George Skelton (LA Times columnist, "Yes")
- Opponents: Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones, Assemblymember Joe Patterson (Republicans), SCNG editorial boards (LA Daily News, Press-Telegram, OC Register), Bay Area News Group (Mercury News, East Bay Times), Santa Cruz Sentinel, SF Chronicle (No — because of the "recalled official can run to replace themselves" provision and because it doesn't address the signature threshold), Election Integrity Project California

Polling: PPIC Sept 2026: 59% no, 35% yes — faces long odds.

Historical context:
- 2003: Gray Davis recalled; Schwarzenegger elected with 48.6% of replacement vote (in a 135-candidate field).
- 2018: Josh Newman recalled over gas tax vote; Ling Ling Chang replaced him. Newman won it back in 2020, lost in 2024.
- 2021: Newsom recall failed 62-38; Larry Elder led replacement field. Cost $200M+.
- Since 1913: 11 state recalls qualified (9 legislators, 2 governors); 6 resulted in removal (5 legislators, 1 governor).

Key arguments:

FOR (Yes):
1. Majority rule: The current system lets a replacement win with a small plurality — in 2003, Schwarzenegger got 48.6% of the replacement vote but only ~31% of all votes cast in the recall election overall (there were about 9 million votes; Schwarzenegger got ~4.2M... actually let me think: Davis was recalled with 55.4% yes. Total votes ~9.5M. Schwarzenegger got 4.2M, which is about 44-48% of replacement votes and ~46% of yes votes...). In 2021, Elder had 49% of replacement vote among those who answered question 2, but because many Newsom-supporting voters skipped Q2 (or wrote in), if the recall had succeeded, Elder would have become governor with ~28% of all votes cast. That's the strongest argument: someone can become governor with a fraction of the vote while the incumbent had support of 38%+... wait, actually in 2021, Newsom kept office with 61.9% voting no on recall. If it had flipped slightly, Elder would be governor with ~28-38% support.
2. The two-question setup is confusing and unusual — only 6 other states use it (per NCSL via the Chronicle).
3. Recall incentive for "gamesmanship": partisan operatives can use recalls as a redo mechanism, targeting "weak gazelles."
4. Aligns replacement process with normal vacancy process (succession for governor, appointments for constitutional officers, special elections for legislators) — consistency.
5. Removes celebrity circus dynamics (135 candidates in 2003, 46 in 2021).
6. Reduces costs in some scenarios (no replacement candidate list to print; gubernatorial special elections consolidated with scheduled elections).

AGAINST (No):
1. Takes away voters' right to choose the replacement — power shifts to the Governor (appointments for constitutional officers) — the party in power picks.
2. Legislative vacancies → special elections → months without representation + extra costs (millions).
3. Recalled official can run to replace themselves — bizarre provision even the author couldn't explain (Chronicle). The old constitutional ban on the recalled officer being a candidate is removed.
4. Partisan motive: authored by a Democrat who was himself recalled after voting for the gas tax ("Newman's Revenge"); placed by Democratic supermajority; likely to benefit the majority party by discouraging recalls.
5. The recall is already rare (11 since 1913) and rarely misused; "if it ain't broke, don't fix it."
6. It doesn't fix the actual problem (low signature threshold, cost) — the Chronicle notes the signature threshold is among the lowest in the nation, and Prop 5 doesn't touch that.
7. For a governor's recall in the first two years: voters' replacement choice is effectively the Lt. Gov., who was elected separately (not necessarily the voters' choice for THIS office at this time) — though the Lt. Gov. is a statewide-elected official.
8. Polling shows it's likely to fail anyway (59% no), which isn't an argument per se.

Also note: partisan asymmetry. In the current era, recalls have been used more by Republicans against Democrats (Newman, Newsom) in California. Making recalls less attractive tends to benefit Democrats. But the same structural argument would apply to any state.

Also worth noting the interesting cross-endorsements: Dan Schnur (a Republican, former FPPC chair) supports Yes. Good-government groups (LWV, Common Cause) support Yes. Republican legislators and conservative editorial boards oppose. Progressive-but-reformist SF Chronicle opposes due to the self-candidacy provision.

There's also a historical note: In 2024, the Legislature put SCA 1 on the 2026 ballot. Actually, there was also an earlier attempt — in 2022, similar measures died. And there was ACA? Let me not worry too much.

One more thing to verify: the claim in the pro argument that "nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money" and "$200 million" cost. The cost was ~$200-276M (state + county). Fine.

I'm going to recommend... Let me think about which produces better outcomes on balance.

Case YES (my evaluation):
1. Majority-rule fix: real, important. California is a democratic outlier with the two-question recall. In 2021, a party that lost the prior election nearly gained the governorship via a candidate with a fraction of the vote. In a 50/50-ish state nationally, imagine a governor removed with 50.5% and replaced by someone with 27% of the total vote — governed by someone 73% didn't choose... well, actually under Prop 5 the Lt. Gov. also wasn't chosen by 50.5%... they were chosen by however they got elected. But the Lt. Gov. IS a statewide-elected official; their election was a regular, majority-legitimate contest... well, actually Lt. Gov. elections in CA are also plurality (top-two runoff = majority-ish). In 2021, Newsom won 2018 with 62%, Kounalakis won with ~58%. Elder would've had ~37% of ballots cast. So legitimacy-wise: Kounalakis 58% vs Elder 37% (of ballots cast in the recall). The succession route produces officeholders with broader mandates.

2. Anti-gamesmanship: Removing the successor question reduces the incentive for partisan recall attempts aimed at seat-flipping rather than genuine removal. DeMaio's "weak gazelle" strategy is exhibit A. The 2021 recall was funded partly as a redo of the 2018 election. 

3. Consistency with vacancy rules: constitutional offices already filled this way on death/resignation.

4. Gubernatorial special election design is thoughtful: consolidated with scheduled elections, majority + runoff, so no extra standalone cost and better legitimacy.

Case NO (my evaluation):
1. Self-candidacy provision: undermines the recall's purpose; unexplained by author; Chronicle's dealbreaker. If a recalled legislator can just win the seat back months later, the recall loses meaning, and special elections have low turnout — an organized incumbent-adjacent candidate could win.
2. Voter power → gubernatorial appointment for constitutional officers: The people lose the direct replacement vote; the Governor gains a patronage opportunity in the middle of a political fight. Though the appointee faces election later.
3. Legislative vacancy/delay/cost: months unrepresented, millions per standalone special election.
4. Self-interested origin: authored by a recalled politician, party-line vote, no campaign even mounted for it.
5. Rarity of problem: 11 recalls since 1913; 2 gubernatorial ever. The current system's "flaw" produced outcomes voters accepted (2003: Schwarzenegger won decisively with 48.6%; 2021: recall defeated 62-38). 

Hmm. Both cases are strong. The deciding factors for me:

(a) The self-candidacy provision is a genuine design flaw that undermines the measure's own stated purpose. But note: it mainly matters for legislative recalls. Actually wait — it also matters for gubernatorial recalls in the first two years (the recalled governor could run in the special election). But by then the voters just voted to remove them... and would vote again within months in a scheduled primary. It's weird but bounded.

(b) The polling (59% no) and the absence of any campaign. Not a merits argument.

(c) The good-government consensus (LWV, Common Cause, Weber, Schnur, McClatchy, Skelton) is Yes. The No side is largely the Republican caucus + conservative boards + the Chronicle on one narrow ground. In terms of nonpartisan expert opinion, Yes has more weight. BUT — careful. The LWV and Common Cause are generally aligned with the Democratic-leaning reform community; their support is meaningful but not neutral.

(d) Which failure mode is worse? Current system's failure: a minority-mandate successor seizes a top office (bad, high-stakes when it's the governor). Prop 5's failure modes: (i) recalled official returns via special election (annoying, but voters' choice); (ii) Governor appoints a partisan replacement (moderately bad, but temporary + regular election follows); (iii) legislative vacancy (annoying but standard vacancy practice); (iv) Lt. Gov. finishes governor's term (standard succession practice, mirrors federal).

Actually, thinking about it more, Prop 5's failure modes are mostly "the same things that happen whenever offices go vacant," while the current system's failure mode is unique to recalls and genuinely destabilizing (minority-rule governor). Also, the gamesmanship point: the two-question format is precisely what makes recalls attractive as power-grabs. E.g., 2021: the recall was polling competitively early on precisely because replacement candidates gave partisans a reason to vote yes ("vote him out AND pick our guy"). 

Hmm, one counterpoint to the gamesmanship argument: the signature threshold is the real entry point for recalls (12% of last turnout), and Prop 5 doesn't raise it. But the replacement question is what makes the recall lucrative.

I'm going to go with YES. Reasons: majority-rule principle (the strongest and most-cited argument, endorsed by the full spectrum of good-government groups and the state's election chief); consistency with existing vacancy succession; removal of the partisan-gamesmanship incentive; and the failure modes of Prop 5 are bounded and mirror standard practice. The self-candidacy quirk is odd but its practical effect is to let voters decide again — which, in a democracy, is defensible, and it applies only to special elections, not appointments.

Wait, but let me reconsider the "Newman's revenge" and self-interested origin once more. Is that a reason to vote no? The Legislature (elected by the people) put it on the ballot; voters get the final say. The origin story is unflattering but the policy is judged on its merits. The same could be said of many reforms.

And let me reconsider the Chronicle's argument once more: "the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure." There's a school of thought that says: never pass constitutional amendments with unexplained provisions, because constitutional changes are hard to reverse. The provision: "the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office" — this actually ADDS a protection (recalled official can't be appointed). And removes the ban on being a candidate. The net effect is ambiguous. I judge the policy net-effect as modestly positive on balance.

Also note: the legislative analysis (LAO) is neutral on net fiscal impact.

Also worth mentioning in my answer: the polling shows it's trailing badly, so a Yes vote is an underdog vote; but that shouldn't determine the vote.

Hmm, actually, hold on. Let me reconsider whether the user might be asking about the 2024 Prop 5 (the housing bond measure), because they might have an old link or cached page. The URL they gave — https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/ — resolves TODAY to the 2026 guide (Prop 5 = recall process). The 2024 Prop 5 was on the November 5, 2024 ballot, and the results are already in (it failed 55-45). Given the current date (the tools suggest we're in 2026, since the 2026 guide is live and dated editorials from Oct/Nov 2026 are appearing), the relevant measure is the 2026 recall one. I'll answer on that, but briefly note the 2024 confusion in case.

Actually, let me make sure about the current date. The editorial pages show dates up to Nov 2, 2026. The PPIC poll was "early September 2026." The SOS measure contributions page says "as of 10/22/2026." So we're at or just after Nov 2-3, 2026, i.e., right at Election Day. The user is deciding how to vote NOW. Good — the 2026 recall Prop 5 is the right target.

Let me do one more round of research to be thorough: (1) the KPBS piece for arguments, (2) the Sac Bee endorsement in full, (3) the LA Times Barabak column, and (4) the PPIC poll page. Then I'll write my answer.","format":"unknown","index":0}]
